source: Selectively adapted catalogue content from AnaxiGraph 0.9.1, Apache-2.0; no legacy scoring or runtime imported.

cards.name: Callback Hell
cards.intent: Identify deeply nested asynchronous callbacks with fragmented errors and control flow.
questions: Can the sequence be represented as one explicit asynchronous workflow with one error boundary?
benefits: Surfaces unreadable sequencing and fragmented failure handling.
liabilities: Flattening syntax does not fix missing cancellation or transaction semantics.
verify: Completion, error, cancellation, and callback ordering remain equivalent.

cards.name: Chain of Responsibility
cards.intent: Pass a request through ordered handlers until one handles it or the chain ends.
questions: Is handler ordering explicit and does exactly one handler normally own the result?
benefits: Decouples senders from a configurable handler sequence.
liabilities: Requests can silently fall through and ordering can become fragile.
verify: Termination and unhandled-request behavior are explicit and tested.

cards.name: Workflow Choreography
cards.intent: Coordinate a distributed workflow through participant reactions to events without one central controller.
questions: Can each participant make progress from local events without hidden global state?
benefits: Reduces central coordinator coupling and supports local autonomy.
liabilities: End-to-end state, debugging, and change impact become harder to see.
verify: Every business outcome and compensation is derivable from recorded event flows.

cards.name: Command
cards.intent: Represent an action request as a value or object with an explicit execution contract.
questions: Does the action need queuing, logging, retries, undo, or independent dispatch?
benefits: Decouples request creation from execution and makes actions inspectable.
liabilities: One class per trivial action can add ceremony and indirection.
verify: Executing a command preserves the original action's preconditions, effects, and result semantics.

cards.name: Implicit Workflow
cards.intent: Detect a business process spread across callbacks, status checks, and side effects without one inspectable lifecycle.
questions: Where can an operator or developer determine the current process state and valid next steps?
benefits: Surfaces hidden lifecycle and recovery behavior.
liabilities: Centralizing a naturally local flow can create an oversized orchestrator.
verify: Every prior workflow state, transition, timeout, and recovery path remains represented.

cards.name: Interpreter
cards.intent: Represent and evaluate a bounded language or expression grammar explicitly.
questions: Is there a stable, bounded grammar that users or configuration must express?
benefits: Makes grammar, evaluation, and extension rules explicit.
liabilities: A custom language creates parsing, security, tooling, and documentation obligations.
verify: Parsing and evaluation are deterministic, bounded, and reject invalid constructs.

cards.name: Mediator
cards.intent: Centralize a cohesive collaboration protocol so participants do not depend directly on one another.
questions: Is there one collaboration protocol with a clear owner rather than many unrelated interactions?
benefits: Reduces many-to-many participant coupling.
liabilities: The mediator can become a god object if every interaction accumulates there.
verify: Participants communicate through the mediator without losing required direct invariants.

cards.name: Observer
cards.intent: Notify registered dependants when one subject changes without hard-coding each dependant.
questions: Are notifications local, bounded, and independent from the subject's primary invariant?
benefits: Supports multiple local reactions without subject conditionals.
liabilities: Notification order, reentrancy, and lifetime can become implicit.
verify: Subscription lifetime, ordering, and failure isolation are defined.

cards.name: Workflow Orchestrator
cards.intent: Own the sequence, state, and failure policy of one multi-step workflow.
questions: Can the coordinator's responsibility be named as one end-to-end outcome?
benefits: Makes workflow order and recovery policy visible.
liabilities: Can centralize participant logic and become a dependency hub.
verify: The orchestrator owns sequencing but participants retain their local domain invariants.

cards.name: Pipeline
cards.intent: Process data through ordered, independently testable stages with explicit handoff contracts.
questions: Does each stage have a coherent transformation contract and defined failure behavior?
benefits: Makes processing order, reuse, and stage testing explicit.
liabilities: Shared mutable context can turn a pipeline into disguised procedural coupling.
verify: Stage order, handoff schema, short-circuiting, and errors remain explicit.

cards.name: Process Manager
cards.intent: Persist and advance the state of a long-running process across messages and failures.
questions: Must workflow state survive restarts, duplicate messages, and delayed responses?
benefits: Makes durable progress and recovery explicit.
liabilities: Adds persistent state, correlation, timeout, and migration complexity.
verify: Duplicate and reordered inputs cannot produce an invalid process transition.

cards.name: Publish–Subscribe
cards.intent: Distribute events to independently registered subscribers through an explicit channel contract.
questions: Can subscribers fail or lag independently without violating the publisher's transaction?
benefits: Decouples event producers from multiple reactions.
liabilities: Delivery guarantees, schemas, ordering, and observability require explicit design.
verify: Delivery, duplication, ordering, and subscriber failure contracts are documented and tested.

cards.name: Rules Engine
cards.intent: Evaluate a changing set of explicit rules independently from workflow plumbing.
questions: Do rules change independently, require explanation, or need non-developer configuration?
benefits: Makes rule inventory, ordering, and explanations inspectable.
liabilities: A general engine can be harder to understand than direct code.
verify: Rule precedence, conflicts, defaults, and explanations are deterministic.

cards.name: Saga
cards.intent: Coordinate a distributed business transaction through local commits and compensating actions.
questions: Can each committed step be compensated or otherwise reconciled after later failure?
benefits: Makes distributed progress and compensation explicit.
liabilities: Compensation is not rollback and intermediate states become visible.
verify: Every failure point has a tested forward-recovery or compensation path.

cards.name: Visitor
cards.intent: Add operations across a stable object structure without placing each operation on every element type.
questions: Is the element hierarchy stable while new cross-cutting operations are added often?
benefits: Keeps cross-type operations together and avoids polluting element contracts.
liabilities: Adding an element type requires updating every visitor.
verify: Every concrete element dispatches to the matching visitor operation exactly once.

cards.name: Workflow State Machine
cards.intent: Model a process lifecycle with explicit states, events, guards, effects, and terminal outcomes.
questions: Can every valid process state and triggering event be enumerated and persisted?
benefits: Makes transition coverage, retries, and terminal behavior inspectable.
liabilities: State explosion can make the model harder than the workflow.
verify: Only declared transitions run effects and terminal states cannot restart implicitly.

cards.name: Domain Aggregate
cards.intent: Define a consistency boundary with one root controlling mutations to related entities and values.
questions: Which invariants must be enforced atomically and which objects share that lifecycle?
benefits: Makes consistency ownership and mutation entry points explicit.
liabilities: Oversized aggregates serialize unrelated work and load excess data.
verify: All invariant-changing operations pass through the aggregate root.

cards.name: Anemic Domain Model
cards.intent: Identify domain types that expose state while scattering their rules across procedural services.
questions: Are domain invariants enforced near the data or repeatedly reconstructed by callers?
benefits: Reveals missing ownership of domain behavior.
liabilities: Moving behavior into objects can be wrong for a deliberate functional data model.
verify: Refactoring centralizes rules without coupling domain data to infrastructure.

cards.name: Cache-Aside
cards.intent: Let application logic load on miss and explicitly update or invalidate cached data.
questions: Can stale data be bounded and can every write path invalidate the same cache key?
benefits: Keeps caching policy explicit and independent from the source of truth.
liabilities: Miss races and incomplete invalidation can serve stale values.
verify: The authoritative store remains the source of truth and invalidation covers every mutation path.

cards.name: CQRS
cards.intent: Use distinct command and query models when write invariants and read shapes have materially different needs.
questions: Do read and write models have independently valuable shapes, scaling, or consistency requirements?
benefits: Allows focused models and independent optimization for reads and writes.
liabilities: Introduces synchronization, eventual consistency, and duplicate model cost.
verify: Every accepted command has a defined projection path and query staleness contract.

cards.name: Data Mapper
cards.intent: Translate between domain objects and storage records without persistence knowledge in the domain.
questions: Does the domain model need to remain independent of the persistence representation?
benefits: Keeps storage schema changes out of domain behavior.
liabilities: Mapping code can become repetitive and hide expensive loading.
verify: Round trips preserve identity, values, and absent/default distinctions.

cards.name: Event Sourcing
cards.intent: Store an append-only sequence of domain events as the authoritative history of state.
questions: Is complete temporal reconstruction worth permanent event compatibility and projection complexity?
benefits: Preserves audit history and enables new projections from recorded facts.
liabilities: Requires event evolution, replay discipline, and eventual-consistency handling.
verify: Replaying the ordered event stream deterministically reconstructs current state.

cards.name: Identity Map
cards.intent: Ensure one in-memory object instance represents each persistent identity within a unit of work.
questions: Can duplicate instances for one record cause inconsistent mutation or equality?
benefits: Preserves object identity and avoids duplicate loads within a transaction.
liabilities: Extending scope too far increases memory use and stale-instance risk.
verify: A persistent key resolves to one live instance inside the defined scope.

cards.name: Immutable Data
cards.intent: Represent state as values that are replaced rather than mutated after construction.
questions: Can updates return new values without breaking identity or performance constraints?
benefits: Simplifies sharing, concurrency, rollback, and reasoning.
liabilities: Copying large structures can add allocation and conversion cost.
verify: Constructed values never change and updates preserve unchanged fields.

cards.name: Memento
cards.intent: Capture and restore an object's internal state without exposing its representation to clients.
questions: Can all relevant state be captured consistently at one boundary?
benefits: Supports undo or checkpoints while preserving encapsulation.
liabilities: Snapshots can be large, stale, or invalid across schema changes.
verify: Restoring a memento reproduces the captured observable state.

cards.name: Repository Pattern
cards.intent: Expose aggregate-oriented persistence operations through a domain-facing collection contract.
questions: Do callers operate on domain aggregates rather than storage-specific rows and joins?
benefits: Keeps domain workflows independent from persistence mechanics.
liabilities: Generic repositories can obscure useful query capabilities and performance.
verify: Repository operations preserve aggregate identity and declared consistency boundaries.

cards.name: Schema Versioning
cards.intent: Evolve persisted or exchanged data through explicit, testable compatibility versions.
questions: Which readers and stored records must survive each schema change?
benefits: Makes compatibility and migration obligations explicit.
liabilities: Long-lived versions accumulate adapters and test combinations.
verify: Supported old data upgrades deterministically and failed upgrades leave the source recoverable.

cards.name: Shared Mutable State
cards.intent: Identify state mutated by multiple owners without one explicit synchronization or consistency boundary.
questions: Who owns each mutation and what orders concurrent observations?
benefits: Surfaces race, stale-read, and ownership risks.
liabilities: Eliminating sharing can add copying or coordination overhead.
verify: Every mutation has one owner or a proven synchronization protocol.

cards.name: Explicit State Machine
cards.intent: Represent finite states, events, guards, and transitions as a validated lifecycle contract.
questions: Can valid states and events be enumerated without hiding unbounded workflow data?
benefits: Rejects implicit transitions and makes lifecycle coverage testable.
liabilities: A formal machine can overcomplicate a simple monotonic status.
verify: Only declared event/state pairs produce a transition and terminal states remain terminal.

cards.name: Temporal Coupling
cards.intent: Detect operations that must be invoked in an undocumented order for correctness.
questions: Can the valid operation order be encoded by construction, state, or one atomic method?
benefits: Exposes hidden lifecycle preconditions.
liabilities: Encoding every order in types can make flexible workflows rigid.
verify: Invalid order is impossible or rejected with an explicit contract error.

cards.name: Unit of Work
cards.intent: Track a coherent set of changes and commit them as one persistence transaction.
questions: Which changes must succeed or roll back together?
benefits: Makes commit and rollback boundaries explicit.
liabilities: Large units hold resources and increase contention.
verify: Partial failure cannot expose a partially committed unit.

cards.name: Value Object
cards.intent: Model a concept by immutable attributes and value equality rather than identity.
questions: Are two instances with equal attributes interchangeable throughout the domain?
benefits: Centralizes validation and makes domain meaning explicit.
liabilities: Tiny wrappers can add noise when no invariant or meaning exists.
verify: Equality, hashing, serialization, and construction enforce the same value semantics.

cards.name: Command–Query Separation
cards.intent: Keep state-changing operations separate from value-returning observations.
questions: Can callers distinguish mutation from observation without performing the operation?
benefits: Makes effects explicit and queries easier to reason about.
liabilities: Can create awkward duplication when an operation must atomically mutate and report a result.
verify: Queries remain side-effect free and commands preserve all required effects.

cards.name: Duplicated Branch Logic
cards.intent: Identify repeated decision branches whose policy can drift independently.
questions: Do the repeated branches encode one policy or coincidentally similar rules?
benefits: Exposes policy duplication before variants diverge.
liabilities: A forced shared helper can couple rules that should evolve separately.
verify: Every original branch outcome remains represented after consolidation.

cards.name: Exception-Driven Control Flow
cards.intent: Detect routine branching implemented through exceptions rather than explicit outcomes.
questions: Is the exceptional path genuinely rare and outside normal domain outcomes?
benefits: Separates ordinary outcomes from fault propagation.
liabilities: Replacing exceptions can weaken established error contracts.
verify: Fault identity, propagation, and cleanup behavior remain intact.

cards.name: Extract Function
cards.intent: Name and isolate a cohesive portion of an oversized or mixed-responsibility function.
questions: Is there a coherent subtask with a smaller input/output boundary than the original function?
benefits: Creates a named unit with a narrower reason to change.
liabilities: Excess extraction can scatter a linear algorithm across indirections.
verify: The extracted unit preserves ordering, effects, errors, and returned values.

cards.name: Flag Argument
cards.intent: Identify boolean or mode parameters that hide multiple behaviors behind one function name.
questions: Does each flag value represent a separately nameable operation?
benefits: Reveals ambiguous APIs and divergent behavior paths.
liabilities: Splitting a truly orthogonal option can multiply a small API unnecessarily.
verify: Every supported flag combination retains an explicit equivalent operation.

cards.name: Function Composition
cards.intent: Build a transformation by combining small functions with compatible contracts.
questions: Are intermediate contracts stable and meaningful outside the current call chain?
benefits: Makes reusable transformation stages explicit.
liabilities: Can hide control flow and allocation costs behind terse composition.
verify: Composition order and intermediate failure behavior remain explicit and tested.

cards.name: Guard Clause
cards.intent: Exit early for invalid, exceptional, or irrelevant cases so the main path stays flat.
questions: Can exceptional preconditions return before the primary behavior begins?
benefits: Reduces nesting and foregrounds the successful path.
liabilities: Too many exits can obscure cleanup or lifecycle obligations.
verify: All prior precondition outcomes and mandatory cleanup still occur.

cards.name: Hidden Side Effect
cards.intent: Detect functions whose names or contracts conceal mutation, I/O, or external actions.
questions: Would a caller reasonably predict every observed effect from the name and public contract?
benefits: Surfaces surprising effects that complicate reuse and testing.
liabilities: Effect-oriented naming alone does not improve a fundamentally tangled boundary.
verify: Effects become explicit without dropping required mutations or external calls.

cards.name: Long Function
cards.intent: Flag a function whose physical span and decision burden impede local understanding.
questions: Does the function contain multiple independently nameable responsibilities?
benefits: Directs review toward costly local reasoning hotspots.
liabilities: Length alone can misclassify cohesive tables or straightforward serialization.
verify: Any decomposition preserves the original contract and sequence-sensitive behavior.

cards.name: Memoization
cards.intent: Reuse a function result for repeated equivalent inputs when computation dominates storage cost.
questions: Is the result determined solely by a bounded, stable cache key?
benefits: Avoids repeated deterministic work.
liabilities: Adds memory, invalidation, and concurrency concerns.
verify: Cached and uncached execution return equivalent values for the same valid key.

cards.name: Null Object
cards.intent: Represent optional behavior with a safe contract-conforming object instead of repeated null checks.
questions: Can no-op behavior satisfy the contract without concealing meaningful absence?
benefits: Centralizes default behavior and reduces scattered optional checks.
liabilities: Can erase an important distinction between missing and empty behavior.
verify: The null object is substitutable and never fabricates domain state.

cards.name: Parameter Clump
cards.intent: Detect a recurring group of values that travels together without a named concept.
questions: Do these parameters share invariants, identity, or a lifecycle worthy of a type?
benefits: Reveals missing domain or configuration concepts.
liabilities: A wrapper with no invariant can merely add ceremony.
verify: Grouping parameters preserves call semantics and validates any shared invariants once.

cards.name: Parameter Object
cards.intent: Name and validate a cohesive set of parameters passed through multiple operations.
questions: Does the proposed object own shared meaning or invariants beyond transport convenience?
benefits: Shortens call sites and creates one place for shared validation.
liabilities: Can become a mutable grab bag if unrelated options accumulate.
verify: All callers retain equivalent defaults and validation behavior.

cards.name: Pure Function
cards.intent: Compute outputs solely from explicit inputs without observable mutation or I/O.
questions: Can every dependency that affects the result be represented as an explicit input?
benefits: Improves composability, deterministic testing, and safe reuse.
liabilities: Pushing unavoidable effects outward can overcomplicate a simple boundary.
verify: Equal valid inputs produce equal outputs and no external state changes.

cards.name: Specification
cards.intent: Represent a composable business predicate as a named, testable rule.
questions: Is the predicate a reusable domain rule rather than a one-off implementation detail?
benefits: Makes policy composition and explanation explicit.
liabilities: Objectifying trivial predicates can bury readable conditions.
verify: Composed specifications preserve truth tables and short-circuit expectations.

cards.name: Table-Driven Dispatch
cards.intent: Replace repetitive key-to-action branches with a bounded declarative lookup.
questions: Do branches differ mainly by stable data or callable selection?
benefits: Makes supported cases enumerable and reduces repetitive branching.
liabilities: A table can obscure complex branch-specific control flow.
verify: Unknown keys and every previously supported case retain defined behavior.

cards.name: Actor Model
cards.intent: Isolate mutable state behind independently scheduled actors that communicate through messages.
questions: Can each stateful entity own its state and progress using explicit messages?
benefits: Localizes mutable state and replaces shared-memory coordination with message boundaries.
liabilities: Mailbox growth, supervision, ordering, and distributed debugging require explicit policies.
verify: Messages, mailbox ordering, actor lifecycle, and failure supervision are deterministic and bounded.

cards.name: Bulkhead
cards.intent: Partition finite resources so failure or saturation in one workload cannot exhaust every peer.
questions: Which independent workload must retain capacity when another becomes slow or overloaded?
benefits: Contains saturation and preserves capacity for independent workloads.
liabilities: Static partitions can strand capacity or hide an undersized system.
verify: Each partition has bounded capacity, observable rejection, and independent recovery.

cards.name: Circuit Breaker
cards.intent: Stop repeated calls to a failing dependency and probe deliberately for recovery.
questions: Can repeated dependency failures be short-circuited without violating correctness?
benefits: Limits cascading latency and gives dependencies time to recover.
liabilities: Poor thresholds create oscillation, false trips, or prolonged rejection.
verify: Closed, open, and probe transitions are observable, bounded, and concurrency safe.

cards.name: Idempotency Key
cards.intent: Associate a stable request identity with a side effect so duplicate delivery produces one logical outcome.
questions: What stable identity and retention window define the same logical request?
benefits: Makes safe retries possible across uncertain transport outcomes.
liabilities: Key scope, expiry, response replay, and storage races must be designed.
verify: Concurrent duplicates share one committed outcome and conflicting key reuse is rejected.

cards.name: Transactional Inbox
cards.intent: Record received message identities transactionally before applying their effects.
questions: Can receipt identity and consumer effects commit within the same atomic boundary?
benefits: Prevents duplicate message effects under redelivery and consumer restart.
liabilities: Retention, cleanup, poisoned messages, and identity scope add operational work.
verify: Receipt and effects commit atomically, and replay cannot repeat the logical effect.

cards.name: Leader Election
cards.intent: Select one current coordinator among competing instances using a time-bounded authority contract.
questions: Which operation truly needs one coordinator, and how is stale authority fenced?
benefits: Coordinates singleton responsibilities while permitting failover.
liabilities: Clock, lease, partition, and stale-leader errors can produce split brain.
verify: Authority expires, stale leaders are fenced, and failover does not overlap unsafe work.

cards.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control
cards.intent: Detect conflicting updates by comparing a version at commit time instead of holding a lock.
questions: Can callers retry or reconcile a rejected update from a fresh version?
benefits: Avoids long-held locks while preventing silent lost updates.
liabilities: High contention causes retries and application-level conflict handling.
verify: Every write compares the expected version atomically and exposes conflicts explicitly.

cards.name: Transactional Outbox
cards.intent: Commit a durable message record with local state, then publish it asynchronously.
questions: Can the local change and publication intent share one transaction?
benefits: Eliminates the gap between committing local state and requesting publication.
liabilities: Relay lag, ordering, cleanup, and duplicate publication remain operational concerns.
verify: State and outbox record commit atomically, and relay publication is idempotently consumable.

cards.name: Pessimistic Locking
cards.intent: Acquire exclusive or constrained access before mutating a contended resource.
questions: Is contention high enough that bounded blocking is safer than repeated reconciliation?
benefits: Prevents concurrent conflicting changes before they occur.
liabilities: Deadlocks, convoying, starvation, and leaked locks can reduce availability.
verify: Lock scope and order are fixed, waits are bounded, and release is guaranteed.

cards.name: Producer–Consumer
cards.intent: Decouple work creation from processing through a bounded transfer channel.
questions: What capacity, ordering, ownership, and shutdown semantics govern the handoff?
benefits: Allows independent pacing and controlled parallel processing.
liabilities: An unbounded channel merely relocates overload into memory or latency.
verify: Capacity, backpressure, cancellation, drain, and item ownership are explicit.

cards.name: Race Condition
cards.intent: Identify results that depend unintentionally on timing or interleaving between concurrent operations.
questions: Which interleavings can violate the target's stated invariant?
benefits: Surfaces timing-dependent correctness failures before choosing a remedy.
liabilities: Adding a broad lock can mask the race while introducing deadlocks or latency.
verify: Every shared transition is atomic, ordered, isolated, or safely commutative.

cards.name: Retry with Backoff
cards.intent: Retry a classified transient failure with bounded attempts, increasing delay, and jitter.
questions: Which errors are transient, and is repeating the operation demonstrably safe?
benefits: Absorbs brief dependency failures without synchronized retry storms.
liabilities: Retries amplify overload and latency when failures are permanent or unsafe to repeat.
verify: Attempts, total time, jitter, cancellation, and retryable errors are bounded and observable.

cards.name: Single Flight
cards.intent: Coalesce concurrent equivalent requests so one operation computes and shares the result.
questions: What key proves requests are equivalent, and may all waiters share errors and cancellation?
benefits: Prevents request stampedes and duplicate expensive computation.
liabilities: A slow leader can delay every waiter and shared cancellation semantics are subtle.
verify: Equivalent in-flight calls have one owner, bounded waiters, and explicit result/error fanout.

cards.name: Timeout
cards.intent: Bound how long an operation may consume caller time or resources.
questions: What deadline reflects the caller's remaining budget and what happens to abandoned work?
benefits: Bounds latency and resource retention across uncertain operations.
liabilities: Timeouts can abandon work that still commits and can obscure the actual overload source.
verify: Deadlines propagate, cancellation is handled, and late outcomes cannot corrupt caller state.

cards.name: Unbounded Concurrency
cards.intent: Detect work creation that can exceed finite processing, memory, connection, or downstream capacity.
questions: Which finite resource limits safe parallelism and how is overload signaled upstream?
benefits: Surfaces overload paths that pass tests but collapse under production volume.
liabilities: An arbitrary semaphore can lower throughput without establishing end-to-end backpressure.
verify: Queued plus active work has a measured bound and rejected work has explicit semantics.

cards.name: Work Queue
cards.intent: Distribute independent jobs from a durable or bounded queue across competing workers.
questions: Are jobs independent, and what are the lease, retry, poison, ordering, and duplicate contracts?
benefits: Smooths bursts and scales independent processing horizontally.
liabilities: Delivery semantics, visibility timeouts, poison jobs, and queue lag require operations.
verify: Every accepted job reaches completion or a visible terminal state without unsafe duplicate effects.

cards.name: Acyclic Dependencies
cards.intent: Organize module dependencies as a directed acyclic graph with explicit dependency direction.
questions: Can the cycle be broken at a stable contract without duplicating state or workflow?
benefits: Enables independent reasoning, testing, and release ordering.
liabilities: Artificial interfaces can merely hide a conceptual cycle.
verify: The resulting module graph has no directed cycle and behavior remains reachable.

cards.name: Anti-Corruption Layer
cards.intent: Translate between bounded models so an external or legacy model does not leak into the local domain.
questions: Do the two sides use materially different concepts, invariants, or lifecycles?
benefits: Protects local domain language from external model churn.
liabilities: Translation can be expensive and duplicate similar representations.
verify: External concepts enter the local model only through explicit translations.

cards.name: Circular Dependency
cards.intent: Identify modules that depend on one another through a directed cycle.
questions: Which shared responsibility or inverted dependency creates the smallest honest cut?
benefits: Surfaces coupled build, initialization, and change ordering.
liabilities: Breaking the graph without fixing ownership can create forwarding modules.
verify: The cycle is absent from resolved dependencies and initialization remains deterministic.

cards.name: Cohesive Module
cards.intent: Group behavior and data that serve one focused responsibility and change together.
questions: Can the module's purpose be stated as one responsibility with one primary reason to change?
benefits: Improves placement, navigation, ownership, and focused testing.
liabilities: Overly narrow modules create fragmented call chains.
verify: Every public symbol supports the declared module responsibility.

cards.name: Dependency Hub
cards.intent: Identify a module whose excessive inbound or outbound dependencies make it a change and failure nexus.
questions: Is the hub cohesive and stable, or does it aggregate unrelated dependencies for convenience?
benefits: Highlights blast-radius and architecture bottlenecks.
liabilities: Fan counts alone can penalize legitimate stable foundations.
verify: Any decomposition reduces dependency breadth without duplicating policy.

cards.name: Dependency Injection
cards.intent: Supply dependencies from a composition boundary instead of constructing them inside behavior.
questions: Does external construction improve substitution or merely move a private detail outward?
benefits: Makes dependencies explicit and supports controlled substitution.
liabilities: A large container can hide wiring and runtime requirements.
verify: Required dependencies are complete at construction and lifecycle ownership is explicit.

cards.name: Feature Envy
cards.intent: Detect behavior that depends more on another module's data and contracts than its own responsibility.
questions: Would moving the behavior improve cohesion without exposing the target module's internals?
benefits: Reveals misplaced behavior and weak ownership.
liabilities: Orchestration legitimately coordinates several collaborators.
verify: Relocation preserves dependency direction and does not broaden internal visibility.

cards.name: God Module
cards.intent: Identify a module that owns many unrelated symbols, effects, and architecture roles.
questions: Which symbol groups change for distinct reasons and have stable boundaries between them?
benefits: Finds concentrated ownership and change risk.
liabilities: Splitting by file size alone can create low-value forwarding layers.
verify: Each extracted module has a cohesive contract and no behavior is duplicated.

cards.name: Information Hiding
cards.intent: Hide volatile decisions behind a stable, minimal module contract.
questions: Which design decision is likely to change and which callers truly need to observe it?
benefits: Contains volatility and reduces accidental coupling.
liabilities: Excessive hiding can prevent necessary optimization or extension.
verify: Internal changes do not require client changes within the supported contract.

cards.name: Package by Feature
cards.intent: Organize modules around user or domain capabilities rather than horizontal technical layers alone.
questions: Do changes for one capability currently cross many technical packages?
benefits: Localizes capability changes and clarifies ownership.
liabilities: Shared technical policy can become duplicated across feature packages.
verify: Feature boundaries preserve shared contracts and avoid reverse dependency leaks.

cards.name: Plugin Architecture
cards.intent: Extend a stable core through discoverable, isolated implementations of explicit extension contracts.
questions: Are extensions independently developed or deployed against a genuinely stable contract?
benefits: Allows optional capabilities without core conditionals.
liabilities: Discovery, compatibility, isolation, and versioning add operational cost.
verify: A plugin can be added or removed without changing core behavior or source.

cards.name: Ports and Adapters
cards.intent: Keep application policy behind inward-facing ports with external technologies implemented as adapters.
questions: Can application behavior run independently of UI, database, network, and framework choices?
benefits: Protects core policy and creates testable technology boundaries.
liabilities: Ports around stable one-off details add ceremony without flexibility.
verify: Dependencies point inward and adapters alone know external technology contracts.

cards.name: Public Module Facade
cards.intent: Expose a deliberate module API while keeping internal file and symbol layout private.
questions: Which operations are supported contracts rather than reachable implementation details?
benefits: Stabilizes imports and allows internal decomposition.
liabilities: An overbroad facade becomes another dependency hub.
verify: Consumers use only the declared facade and supported names remain compatible.

cards.name: Separated Interface
cards.intent: Place a contract in the module that owns the need while implementations live behind the dependency boundary.
questions: Which side owns the abstraction's meaning and stability requirements?
benefits: Inverts dependencies without moving implementation ownership.
liabilities: Contracts can drift from implementation capabilities if ownership is unclear.
verify: The consumer-owned interface contains no implementation-specific types.

cards.name: Shotgun Surgery
cards.intent: Identify one conceptual change that repeatedly requires small edits across many modules.
questions: What policy or data definition is duplicated across the files that change together?
benefits: Reveals missing ownership and costly change propagation.
liabilities: Change count without commit coupling can overstate the pattern.
verify: A representative change becomes localized without creating a central god module.

cards.name: Stable Dependencies
cards.intent: Direct dependencies toward modules that are more stable and abstract than their consumers.
questions: Does a stable policy module currently depend on a more volatile detail?
benefits: Reduces propagation from volatile details into stable policy.
liabilities: Stability metrics can lag a deliberate architectural transition.
verify: Dependency direction matches ownership and does not introduce a cycle.

cards.name: Abstract Factory
cards.intent: Create compatible families of related objects without coupling clients to concrete classes.
questions: Must clients switch an entire compatible product family together?
benefits: Centralizes family selection and prevents incompatible product combinations.
liabilities: Adding a new product role can require changing every factory implementation.
verify: Each factory yields a mutually compatible product family.

cards.name: Adapter
cards.intent: Translate an existing interface into the contract expected by a client.
questions: Is this boundary translating contracts rather than adding new business policy?
benefits: Contains external or legacy interface differences.
liabilities: Can become a dumping ground for unrelated policy and validation.
verify: Every adapted operation preserves source semantics and target contract expectations.

cards.name: Bridge
cards.intent: Separate an abstraction from an independently varying implementation hierarchy.
questions: Do abstraction and implementation represent two genuinely independent dimensions of change?
benefits: Avoids a combinatorial subclass hierarchy.
liabilities: Adds indirection when only one dimension actually varies.
verify: Every supported abstraction remains compatible with every permitted implementation.

cards.name: Builder
cards.intent: Assemble an object whose construction has many optional parts, step by step.
questions: Does a caller have to remember an assembly order the constructor does not enforce?
benefits: Names each optional part and keeps half-built objects out of reach.
liabilities: A language with keyword arguments, defaults, or dataclasses often expresses this with no builder at all; adding one then buys ceremony, not clarity.
verify: An object built through the builder is indistinguishable from one built directly.

cards.name: Composite
cards.intent: Treat individual objects and recursive groups through one common interface.
questions: Can clients apply the same meaningful operation to leaves and containers?
benefits: Makes recursive structures uniform for callers.
liabilities: A broad common interface can force meaningless operations onto leaves.
verify: Container behavior is the defined composition of child behavior.

cards.name: Decorator
cards.intent: Add composable behavior around an object while retaining its contract.
questions: Is the added responsibility independently optional and order-aware?
benefits: Supports runtime composition without subclass explosion.
liabilities: Many wrappers can obscure execution order and identity.
verify: The wrapped object remains substitutable and decoration order is tested.

cards.name: Dependency Inversion
cards.intent: Make high-level policy depend on stable abstractions rather than volatile implementation details.
questions: Is there a volatile dependency with multiple implementations or a boundary worth isolating?
benefits: Stabilizes policy code across infrastructure changes.
liabilities: Speculative interfaces increase navigation and configuration cost.
verify: High-level behavior is testable against the abstraction and no implementation detail leaks through.

cards.name: Facade
cards.intent: Offer a focused entry point over a more complex subsystem.
questions: Can the subsystem's common use cases be expressed through one cohesive boundary?
benefits: Reduces client coupling and reveals supported workflows.
liabilities: A facade can grow into an oversized service that owns unrelated behavior.
verify: Facade operations preserve subsystem contracts and do not conceal required advanced access.

cards.name: Factory Method
cards.intent: Delegate construction choice while keeping the creation protocol stable.
questions: Does construction vary independently from the operation that uses the object?
benefits: Localizes concrete construction decisions.
liabilities: Subclass-based creation can be heavier than passing a callable.
verify: Every factory result satisfies the declared product contract.

cards.name: Flyweight
cards.intent: Share one immutable instance across many uses instead of repeating it.
questions: Is there a measured memory cost, and is the shared state truly immutable?
benefits: Removes duplicated immutable state when the duplication is measured.
liabilities: Without a measurement this is premature: it adds a lookup and a lifetime question to save memory nobody showed was scarce. Sharing anything mutable turns it into a defect.
verify: Shared instances are immutable, and behaviour is identical with sharing switched off.

cards.name: God Object
cards.intent: Identify a type that centralizes many unrelated responsibilities and collaborators.
questions: Which responsibilities change for different reasons or serve different callers?
benefits: Surfaces concentrated change risk and low cohesion.
liabilities: Mechanical splitting can create chatty objects and broken invariants.
verify: Any split retains ownership of cross-responsibility invariants and transaction boundaries.

cards.name: Inappropriate Inheritance
cards.intent: Detect subtype relationships used for reuse despite weak substitutability.
questions: Can every subtype honor the base contract without disabling or redefining operations?
benefits: Exposes fragile reuse and violated substitutability.
liabilities: Replacing inheritance can lose framework-required extension semantics.
verify: Every replacement preserves polymorphic behavior expected by current clients.

cards.name: Iterator
cards.intent: Walk a collection without exposing how it is stored.
questions: Do callers depend on how the collection is stored rather than on its order?
benefits: Lets the storage change without touching every caller.
liabilities: Python, JavaScript and TypeScript all have an iteration protocol and generators; a hand-written iterator class is usually the idiom written the long way.
verify: Callers see the same sequence when the underlying storage is replaced.

cards.name: Leaky Abstraction
cards.intent: Identify an abstraction that forces callers to understand hidden implementation details.
questions: Can callers use the abstraction correctly without knowing the selected implementation?
benefits: Reveals boundaries that fail to contain volatility.
liabilities: Some operational characteristics cannot or should not be hidden.
verify: The repaired contract exposes necessary capabilities without implementation-specific coupling.

cards.name: Prototype
cards.intent: Produce a new object by copying a configured instance instead of rebuilding it.
questions: Is construction genuinely expensive, and is the copy's depth defined?
benefits: Avoids repeating costly setup when instances differ only slightly.
liabilities: Most languages ship copying already, and a hand-written clone tends to drift from the fields it must copy. Shallow and deep copies fail differently.
verify: A copy shares exactly the state the contract says it shares, and no more.

cards.name: Provider Abstraction
cards.intent: Define one stable provider contract for multiple interchangeable external or model implementations.
questions: Do at least two real providers share stable semantics, lifecycle, and error expectations?
benefits: Removes provider conditionals from clients and supports runtime substitution.
liabilities: A lowest-common-denominator interface can hide provider-specific capabilities.
verify: Every provider passes the same contract suite and records provider-specific provenance separately.

cards.name: Proxy
cards.intent: Control access to another object while preserving its client-facing contract.
questions: Is the added behavior access control, location, caching, or lifecycle rather than domain policy?
benefits: Encapsulates access concerns behind a substitutable boundary.
liabilities: Remote or lazy behavior can make cost and failure less visible.
verify: Proxy-visible behavior matches the subject contract including error semantics.

cards.name: Singleton
cards.intent: Identify one globally reachable mutable instance that callers cannot substitute.
questions: Can a test substitute this, and what happens when two of them exist?
benefits: Names a dependency that cannot be replaced, which is what makes it hard to test.
liabilities: Recorded as a failure mode, not a recommendation: it hides a dependency, serialises unrelated work, and outlives the scope that needed it. A module-level value or an injected instance is usually the smaller answer.
verify: Every caller can be handed a substitute without changing its code.

cards.name: State
cards.intent: Delegate behavior to explicit state objects when valid operations vary by lifecycle state.
questions: Are states stable domain concepts with distinct behavior and transition rules?
benefits: Localizes state-specific behavior and transitions.
liabilities: Creates many types for a small or mostly data-driven lifecycle.
verify: Only declared transitions occur and every state preserves shared invariants.

cards.name: Strategy
cards.intent: Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms behind one stable operation contract.
questions: Do multiple real algorithms solve the same problem under the same preconditions?
benefits: Makes algorithm selection explicit and removes caller conditionals.
liabilities: Adds object and configuration overhead for trivial variation.
verify: All strategies satisfy shared inputs, outputs, errors, and domain invariants.

cards.name: Template Method
cards.intent: Fix an algorithm skeleton while allowing selected steps to vary through overrides.
questions: Is the invariant sequence more stable than the individual customizable steps?
benefits: Keeps workflow order centralized while exposing narrow extension points.
liabilities: Inheritance couples extensions to lifecycle and protected implementation details.
verify: Overrides cannot bypass mandatory steps or shared cleanup.

cards.name: Assertion Roulette
cards.intent: Identify tests with many weakly identified assertions whose failure does not reveal the broken behavior.
questions: Does each failure identify one behavior and the input that violated it?
benefits: Surfaces tests that detect failure but make diagnosis unnecessarily expensive.
liabilities: Splitting every assertion can duplicate expensive setup and obscure one cohesive invariant.
verify: Each assertion failure names the behavior, case, and relevant expected outcome.

cards.name: Backpressure
cards.intent: Propagate finite downstream capacity toward producers before queues or resources become unbounded.
questions: How does every producer observe and respond to downstream saturation?
benefits: Keeps memory, latency, and active work within explicit capacity.
liabilities: Blocking or rejecting at one boundary is ineffective if upstream continues buffering elsewhere.
verify: Capacity is bounded end to end and overload has a documented block, shed, or degrade outcome.

cards.name: Characterization Test
cards.intent: Capture consequential existing behavior before changing code whose intended contract is incomplete.
questions: Which observable behavior must remain stable through the planned change?
benefits: Creates a regression boundary around legacy behavior before refactoring.
liabilities: It can freeze accidental behavior if observations are mistaken for desired requirements.
verify: Tests observe stable public effects and document which captured behaviors are intentional.

cards.name: Contract Test
cards.intent: Verify that independently changing participants agree on an interface's requests, responses, and failure behavior.
questions: Which consumer expectations must every provider version satisfy independently?
benefits: Finds integration incompatibility earlier than full end-to-end environments.
liabilities: Incomplete consumer examples can bless a contract that misses important provider behavior.
verify: The same versioned contract cases execute against consumer expectations and provider behavior.

cards.name: Correlation Identifier
cards.intent: Carry a stable operation identity across asynchronous and remote boundaries for end-to-end diagnosis.
questions: Can every log, message, retry, and downstream call be tied to the same logical operation?
benefits: Makes distributed execution paths searchable without coupling business logic to diagnostics.
liabilities: Unbounded or sensitive identifiers can leak data and create high-cardinality telemetry.
verify: Identifiers propagate across every boundary, are safe to expose, and distinguish retries from new operations.

cards.name: Fail Fast
cards.intent: Reject invalid state or input at the earliest boundary that has enough evidence to decide.
questions: Which boundary first knows the invariant is violated, and can it return actionable context?
benefits: Shortens fault distance and prevents invalid state from spreading.
liabilities: Failing too early can reduce resilience when degradation or aggregation is the real requirement.
verify: Invalid inputs produce deterministic, attributable failures before any forbidden side effect.

cards.name: Flaky Test
cards.intent: Identify a test whose outcome changes without a relevant code or controlled-input change.
questions: Which uncontrolled input, ordering, lifetime, or environmental dependency changes the result?
benefits: Surfaces false signals that erode trust in the entire verification suite.
liabilities: Blind retries hide both flaky tests and intermittent product defects.
verify: Time, randomness, state, concurrency, and external dependencies are controlled or explicitly bounded.

cards.name: Graceful Degradation
cards.intent: Preserve a defined reduced service when a noncritical dependency or capability is unavailable.
questions: Which capability may be omitted, and how will callers know the response is degraded?
benefits: Keeps critical paths available through isolated noncritical failures.
liabilities: Silent fallback can return stale or misleading results and conceal persistent outages.
verify: Degraded results are safe, explicit, observable, and automatically recover when dependencies do.

cards.name: Health Check
cards.intent: Expose distinct evidence that a component is alive and that it is ready to receive useful work.
questions: What minimal local evidence distinguishes liveness from readiness without causing a dependency storm?
benefits: Supports safe traffic routing, restart decisions, and operational diagnosis.
liabilities: Deep checks can overload dependencies; shallow checks can report healthy while useless.
verify: Checks are bounded, side-effect free, and report liveness and readiness independently.

cards.name: Hermetic Test
cards.intent: Make a test result depend only on declared, controlled inputs and isolated resources.
questions: Can time, randomness, filesystem, network, process, and persistent state be owned by the test?
benefits: Improves reproducibility, parallelism, speed, and local diagnosis.
liabilities: Over-isolation can miss deployment and integration failures.
verify: Repeated and parallel runs from a clean environment produce the same result.

cards.name: Property-Based Testing
cards.intent: Generate broad inputs and verify stable properties instead of enumerating only example cases.
questions: Which invariant must hold across the valid input domain, and how will failures shrink?
benefits: Finds edge cases beyond hand-picked examples and documents general invariants.
liabilities: Weak properties, invalid generators, or irreproducible randomness create false confidence.
verify: Generators respect domain constraints and every failure records a reproducible minimal case.

cards.name: Rate Limiter
cards.intent: Constrain admitted operations per identity and time window to protect capacity or policy.
questions: Which identity, capacity, burst, distribution, and fairness semantics define admission?
benefits: Protects finite resources and makes overload policy explicit.
liabilities: Incorrect identity or distributed counters cause unfairness, bypass, or excess rejection.
verify: Admission is bounded, race safe, observable, and returns explicit retry semantics.

cards.name: Structured Logging
cards.intent: Emit machine-queryable events with stable names, fields, context, and severity.
questions: Which operational questions must events answer without parsing prose or exposing secrets?
benefits: Makes behavior searchable, aggregatable, and correlatable across components.
liabilities: Unbounded fields, secrets, duplicate reporting, and excessive volume damage operations.
verify: Event schemas are stable, contextual, redacted, severity-correct, and emitted once at the owning boundary.

cards.name: Test Data Builder
cards.intent: Create valid test objects through intent-revealing defaults and focused overrides.
questions: Can a valid default make each test specify only the fields relevant to its behavior?
benefits: Reduces brittle setup while making variations and invalid cases explicit.
liabilities: Hidden defaults can make tests pass for reasons the reader cannot see.
verify: Defaults are valid and deterministic, and overrides remain visible at the test call site.

cards.name: Test Double
cards.intent: Replace a collaborator with a controlled fake, stub, spy, or mock at a deliberate boundary.
questions: Which collaborator behavior must be controlled, and which implementation details must remain irrelevant?
benefits: Makes rare outcomes deterministic and isolates the unit's own behavior.
liabilities: Interaction-heavy mocks couple tests to implementation and can diverge from real collaborators.
verify: The double implements the relevant contract and tests observable behavior rather than incidental call order.

cards.name: Test Pyramid
cards.intent: Balance many fast focused checks with fewer integration and end-to-end checks at their natural boundaries.
questions: At which cheapest level can each important risk be tested without faking away the behavior?
benefits: Provides fast feedback while retaining confidence at real boundaries.
liabilities: Treating the shape as a quota can produce low-value unit tests and miss integration risk.
verify: Each test level owns distinct risks, and slower suites remain bounded and intentionally selected.

cards.name: Big Ball of Mud
cards.intent: Identify a system whose conceptual boundaries are obscured by pervasive dependencies and opportunistic changes.
questions: Can ownership, change impact, and dependency direction be explained without tracing most of the repository?
benefits: Names systemic coupling that local cleanup alone cannot resolve.
liabilities: A wholesale rewrite usually recreates the same missing boundaries with greater delivery risk.
verify: Improvement is measured through fewer cycles, narrower change fanout, and explicit owned interfaces.

cards.name: Bounded Context
cards.intent: Define a domain boundary within which one model and vocabulary have precise, owned meaning.
questions: Where do language, rules, ownership, and change cadence become meaningfully different?
benefits: Prevents one ambiguous model from coupling distinct business capabilities.
liabilities: Arbitrary boundaries duplicate concepts and create translation overhead without real autonomy.
verify: Each context owns its model and translates explicitly at every cross-context relationship.

cards.name: Branch by Abstraction
cards.intent: Replace an implementation incrementally behind a stable abstraction while keeping the mainline releasable.
questions: Can old and new behavior coexist behind one contract while callers migrate independently?
benefits: Enables small reversible migration steps without a long-lived source branch.
liabilities: A temporary abstraction can become permanent complexity if removal criteria are absent.
verify: Both implementations satisfy the same contract and the old path has an explicit retirement condition.

cards.name: Cell-Based Architecture
cards.intent: Partition a service into repeated, isolated deployment cells with bounded failure and tenant scope.
questions: Is there a stable partition key that permits independent capacity, routing, and failure containment?
benefits: Bounds blast radius and permits incremental regional or tenant scaling.
liabilities: Routing, rebalance, uneven load, duplication, and cross-cell operations add substantial complexity.
verify: A cell failure cannot exhaust peers, and placement plus recovery are deterministic and observable.

cards.name: Clean Architecture
cards.intent: Keep core policy independent from delivery, persistence, frameworks, and other volatile mechanisms.
questions: Can business policy execute and be tested without instantiating delivery or infrastructure frameworks?
benefits: Protects durable policy from volatile external mechanisms.
liabilities: Uniform concentric layers can add interfaces and mapping where no policy boundary exists.
verify: Source dependencies point from mechanisms toward stable policy contracts.

cards.name: Domain-Driven Design
cards.intent: Organize complex software around an evolving domain model, shared language, and explicit context boundaries.
questions: Is domain complexity the primary difficulty, with domain experts able to refine one shared language?
benefits: Aligns code boundaries and terminology with consequential business rules.
liabilities: Applying tactical vocabulary to a simple system creates ceremony without improving understanding.
verify: Models enforce domain invariants and context relationships match real ownership and language boundaries.

cards.name: Event-Driven Architecture
cards.intent: Coordinate components through explicit facts about completed state changes and asynchronous reactions.
questions: Are events immutable domain facts with clear owners, schemas, ordering, and delivery semantics?
benefits: Decouples producers from independently evolving reactions and supports temporal workflows.
liabilities: Eventual consistency, schema evolution, duplicate delivery, and invisible flows raise operating cost.
verify: Events have stable meaning and ownership; consumers are idempotent and observable.

cards.name: Evolutionary Architecture
cards.intent: Guide architecture through incremental change constrained by automated fitness functions.
questions: Which architectural properties must remain measurable as structure and requirements evolve?
benefits: Makes architecture adaptable while protecting explicit quality attributes continuously.
liabilities: Weak or proxy fitness functions can optimize metrics while the real design degrades.
verify: Every critical architecture property has an automated, versioned, actionable fitness function.

cards.name: Hexagonal Architecture
cards.intent: Place application behavior behind explicit ports implemented by inbound and outbound adapters.
questions: Which use-case and collaborator contracts belong to the core, independent of transport and technology?
benefits: Makes core behavior testable and replaceable across delivery and infrastructure mechanisms.
liabilities: Ports for every trivial dependency can fragment navigation and duplicate data shapes.
verify: Core code owns ports and has no source dependency on concrete adapters.

cards.name: Layered Architecture
cards.intent: Group responsibilities into ordered layers with explicit allowed dependency directions.
questions: Do the proposed layers represent stable responsibility levels rather than technical folders alone?
benefits: Provides a simple dependency model and separates broad responsibility categories.
liabilities: Changes cut through every layer and pass-through layers add latency and ceremony.
verify: Allowed layer dependencies are explicit, acyclic, and enforced automatically.

cards.name: Microservices Architecture
cards.intent: Deploy independently owned services around cohesive capabilities with explicit remote contracts.
questions: Which capabilities genuinely require independent ownership, release, scaling, or failure isolation?
benefits: Permits independent evolution and scaling where real autonomy exists.
liabilities: Remote failure, data ownership, observability, deployment, and consistency become mandatory complexity.
verify: Each service owns its data and lifecycle, and cross-service contracts tolerate partial failure.

cards.name: Modular Monolith
cards.intent: Keep deployment unified while enforcing cohesive internal modules with explicit interfaces and owned data.
questions: Can capability boundaries be enforced in one process without requiring independent deployment?
benefits: Preserves simple operations and transactions while enabling clear internal ownership and change isolation.
liabilities: Without automated boundary checks it decays into package names over a coupled monolith.
verify: Modules expose narrow contracts, own data, remain acyclic, and cannot bypass boundaries.

cards.name: Premature Distribution
cards.intent: Identify remote boundaries introduced before independent ownership or runtime needs justify their cost.
questions: What measured autonomy, scale, security, or failure requirement requires this to be a network boundary now?
benefits: Surfaces infrastructure cost that does not buy meaningful independence.
liabilities: Collapsing a justified isolation boundary can reintroduce unacceptable blast radius or coupling.
verify: Every remote boundary maps to a documented owner and measurable independent runtime requirement.

cards.name: Serverless Architecture
cards.intent: Compose managed, event-triggered compute and services where execution can remain stateless and bounded.
questions: Do workload shape and operational goals justify provider limits, cold starts, and managed-service coupling?
benefits: Reduces host operations and scales bounded event work with demand.
liabilities: Execution limits, cold starts, local testing, observability, and vendor coupling constrain design.
verify: Handlers are idempotent, time bounded, stateless between invocations, and observable across managed boundaries.

cards.name: Service-Oriented Architecture
cards.intent: Expose reusable business capabilities through explicit interoperable service contracts.
questions: Which stable business capabilities need interoperable contracts across independently governed systems?
benefits: Creates explicit reusable enterprise capabilities and integration boundaries.
liabilities: Central governance, shared schemas, and generic services can slow change and concentrate coupling.
verify: Contracts have clear owners, versioning, failure semantics, and capability-focused boundaries.

cards.name: Strangler Fig
cards.intent: Replace a legacy system incrementally by routing bounded capabilities to a new implementation.
questions: Which independently observable capability can be intercepted, verified, and retired first?
benefits: Turns a risky replacement into reversible capability-by-capability migration.
liabilities: Dual routing, data synchronization, and a permanent facade can outlive the migration.
verify: Routing is explicit, old and new behavior are compared, and each migrated slice has a retirement criterion.
